characters.name: Nehemiah
characters.perkNote: Bonus themed around organizing and rallying people to a task — mirrors his role uniting builders, guards, treasurers, and reformers throughout the book.

genealogy.note: No wife or children are mentioned anywhere in the book. His brother Hanani (1:2, 7:2) is indexed separately as a submanager. NAMING COLLISION: 'Nehemiah' is not unique to him in this book — distinct from Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, ruler of half of Beth-zur, who repaired a separate wall portion (3:16), and from an earlier, different Nehemiah listed among the leaders of the first return under Zerubbabel (7:7, paralleling Ezra 2:2).

funFacts: Held one of the most sensitive jobs in the Persian court — cupbearer, tasting the king's wine as a safeguard against poisoning (1:11-2:1) — before ever becoming governor of Judah.
Surveyed Jerusalem's ruined walls alone by night, on a donkey, before telling any official in the city why he had come (2:12-16).
As governor he deliberately did NOT claim the standard governor's food allowance for twelve years, feeding many at his own table instead (5:14-18).

verses.note: Hears his brother Hanani's report that Jerusalem's wall is broken down and its gates burned; weeps, mourns, fasts, and prays for days.
Identifies himself as 'the king's cupbearer' just before his petition to Artaxerxes.
Petitions King Artaxerxes in person; granted letters of safe passage and a grant of timber for the gates, the wall, and his own house.
Surveys Jerusalem's broken walls and burned gates by night before revealing his plan to anyone.
Rallies the officials and people to the work: 'Let us rise up and build.'
Answers Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem's mockery directly: 'The God of heaven, he will prosper us... but ye have no portion, nor right, nor memorial, in Jerusalem.'
Sets a watch against the conspiracy to attack the builders and arms the people by families with swords, spears, and bows.
Organizes half the workforce to build and half to guard, keeps arms at hand, and has the men lodge inside Jerusalem for security until the wall is finished.
Personally rebukes the nobles and rulers over usury against the poor, holds a great public assembly, and makes them swear to restore pledges and stop charging interest.
As governor for twelve years, refuses the customary governor's food allowance and feeds many at his own table, 'because of the fear of God.'
Refuses Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem's repeated invitations to meet on the plain of Ono, recognizing it as a plot against him.
Answers Sanballat's open letter accusing him of plotting rebellion/kingship, denying the charge as invention.
Refuses Shemaiah's counsel to hide in the temple, discerning it as a hired scheme meant to make him sin and be discredited.
The wall is finished in fifty-two days, in the month Elul.
Appoints gatekeepers, singers, and Levites, and charges his brother Hanani together with Hananiah, ruler of the palace, with Jerusalem's security.
As 'the Tirshatha,' together with Ezra the priest/scribe and the Levites, tells the weeping people to instead rejoice, eat, drink, and share portions.
The sealed covenant document is headed by his own name and title: 'Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah.'
Personally brings the princes of Judah up onto the wall and appoints two great processional companies of thanksgiving for the dedication.
Walks with the second thanksgiving company along the wall, then stands with them together in the house of God.
On returning from Persia, discovers Eliashib had prepared Tobiah a chamber in the temple courts and personally casts out all of Tobiah's household goods.
Restores the neglected Levite tithes and personally appoints trustworthy treasurers over the storehouses.
Confronts Sabbath-breaking traders, personally shuts Jerusalem's gates before the Sabbath, and warns the merchants away from the walls.
Contends with men who had married foreign wives, rebukes and strikes some of them, and makes them swear an oath to stop.
Drives away a grandson of Eliashib the high priest who had married Sanballat's daughter.

characters.name: Hanani
characters.perkNote: Family loyalty — brings the initial report that starts the whole book and later shares administrative charge of Jerusalem.

genealogy.note: Called 'one of my brethren' (1:2) and 'my brother' (7:2); traditionally read as Nehemiah's literal brother sharing father Hachaliah, though the text does not explicitly restate Hachaliah's name in connection with Hanani.

verses.note: Comes from Judah with other men and reports to Nehemiah the state of the remnant and Jerusalem's ruined walls — the report that triggers the whole book.
Given joint charge over Jerusalem together with Hananiah, ruler of the palace.

characters.name: Hananiah, ruler of the palace
characters.perkNote: Trusted administrative appointee — put in charge of Jerusalem alongside Hanani.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: distinct from at least three other men named Hananiah in this book — the wall-builder 'son of one of the apothecaries' (3:8), the wall-builder 'son of Shelemiah' (3:30), and one of the priests with trumpets at the wall dedication (12:41). The description 'a faithful man, and feared God above many' (7:2) most naturally refers to Hananiah as the nearer antecedent, though the pronoun is grammatically ambiguous and could instead describe Hanani.

verses.note: Appointed ruler of the palace (or 'the castle') and given joint charge over Jerusalem with Hanani; described as faithful and God-fearing above many.

characters.name: Shelemiah the priest
characters.perkNote: One of four treasurers Nehemiah personally appoints over the storehouses because they were counted faithful.

genealogy.note: Possibly, but not confirmably, the same Shelemiah who fathered the wall-builder Hananiah (3:30) — the text does not link the two mentions.

verses.note: Appointed by Nehemiah as one of the treasurers over the storehouses, 'for they were counted faithful.'

characters.name: Zadok the scribe
characters.perkNote: One of four treasurers Nehemiah personally appoints over the storehouses because they were counted faithful.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: at least two other, distinct men named Zadok appear earlier in the book as wall-builders — Zadok son of Baana (3:4) and Zadok son of Immer (3:29). The text does not identify this treasurer as either of them.

verses.note: Appointed by Nehemiah as one of the treasurers over the storehouses.

characters.name: Pedaiah of the Levites
characters.perkNote: One of four treasurers Nehemiah personally appoints over the storehouses because they were counted faithful.

genealogy.note: Distinct from Pedaiah the son of Parosh, a lay wall-builder (3:25) — different family, different role, no textual link between them.

verses.note: Appointed by Nehemiah as one of the treasurers over the storehouses.

characters.name: Hanan, son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah
characters.perkNote: Appointed 'next to their hand' as an assistant among the four treasurers.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: 'Hanan' recurs for several other, apparently distinct men in this book (e.g. among the Levites who helped teach the Law in 8:7, and among covenant-sealers in 10:10,22,26) — none is confirmed as the same person as this treasurer.

verses.note: Appointed as an assistant among the treasurers Nehemiah set over the storehouses.

characters.name: Sanballat the Horonite
characters.perkNote: Thematic 'friction' figure — bonus flavor built around overcoming outside political opposition to progress.

children: an unnamed daughter, married to a grandson of Eliashib the high priest (13:28)
genealogy.note: Only ever called 'Sanballat the Horonite' in this book — no title or office is stated for him directly in the text itself, though he clearly wields real political influence in the region.

funFacts: His mocking question, 'will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?' (4:2), turned out to be exactly what happened.

verses.note: Grieved, along with Tobiah, that someone had come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel.
Laughs Nehemiah and the people to scorn, accusing them of rebelling against the king.
Mocks the rebuilding effort before his brethren and the army of Samaria: 'What do these feeble Jews?'
Conspires with Tobiah, the Arabians, Ammonites, and Ashdodites to fight against Jerusalem and hinder the work.
Repeatedly invites Nehemiah to meet in the plain of Ono, a plot Nehemiah refuses.
Sends an open letter accusing Nehemiah of plotting to rebel and be crowned king, to intimidate him into stopping the work.
Together with Tobiah, hires Shemaiah to try to frighten Nehemiah into a temple offense.
Named in Nehemiah's prayer asking God to remember his and Tobiah's works against him.
His daughter's marriage to a grandson of Eliashib the high priest is discovered and the grandson is driven away by Nehemiah.

characters.name: Geshem the Arabian
characters.perkNote: Recurring co-conspirator alongside Sanballat and Tobiah, always named third and without a distinct action of his own.

genealogy.note: Some extrabiblical Arabian inscriptions of this era have been associated with a 'Geshem/Gashmu' by historians, but Nehemiah's own text gives no further identifying detail beyond 'the Arabian.'

verses.note: Joins Sanballat and Tobiah in laughing the rebuilders to scorn and accusing them of rebellion.
Joins Sanballat in the plot to lure Nehemiah to the plain of Ono.

characters.name: Tobiah the Ammonite
characters.perkNote: Thematic figure for opposition operating through internal alliances, correspondence, and family connections inside Judah rather than open force.

spouses: an unnamed daughter of Shechaniah the son of Arah (6:18)
children: Jehohanan, who married a daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah (6:18)
genealogy.note: Called 'the servant, the Ammonite' (2:10, 2:19) — whether 'servant' denotes an official Persian-administrative title or a status/class marker is not clarified by the text itself. Later 'allied unto' Eliashib the high priest by an unspecified family/relational tie (13:4).

funFacts: Despite being one of the wall's chief opponents, he had enough standing among Jerusalem's own nobles that many of them wrote letters praising him to Nehemiah (6:17-19).

verses.note: Grieved, along with Sanballat, that someone had come to seek the welfare of Israel.
Joins Sanballat and Geshem in mocking and accusing the rebuilders.
Mocks the wall's strength: 'Even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall.'
Joins the conspiracy to fight against Jerusalem.
Joins Sanballat in the repeated invitations to Ono.
Together with Sanballat, hires Shemaiah to try to frighten Nehemiah into a temple offense.

Maintains an active correspondence with many nobles of Judah, who report his good deeds to Nehemiah and carry his letters back, owing to his marriage ties to Shechaniah's family and his son's marriage to Meshullam's daughter.
Given a large chamber in the temple courts by Eliashib the high priest, to whom he was allied; Nehemiah, on discovering this, casts out all his household goods.

characters.name: Shemaiah the son of Delaiah
characters.perkNote: A hired agent of the opposition rather than a family supporter — fits the opposition-flavored perk.

genealogy.note: Full patronymic given as 'Shemaiah the son of Delaiah the son of Mehetabeel' (6:10). NAMING COLLISION: 'Shemaiah' is an extremely common name reused for several other, distinct men elsewhere in this same book (e.g. a wall-builder/gatekeeper in 3:29, and multiple priests among the lists in chapters 10 and 12) — none of those is this hired false prophet. Text states he was hired jointly 'by Tobiah and Sanballat' (6:12-13); attached here to Tobiah since he is named first in that verse, but the hiring is explicitly shared between both men.

verses.note: Shut up in his own house, he urges Nehemiah to hide in the temple claiming assassins are coming by night; Nehemiah discerns Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him to make him sin and be discredited.

characters.name: Noadiah the prophetess
characters.perkNote: No mechanical perk assigned — a single-verse standalone opposition figure, not confirmed as anyone's hired agent.

genealogy.note: Grouped by Nehemiah with 'the rest of the prophets' who tried to frighten him. Unlike Shemaiah, the text does not state she was hired by Tobiah or Sanballat, so no submanager relationship to them is asserted here. NAMING COLLISION: shares her name with an unrelated male Levite, Noadiah the son of Binnui (Ezra 8:33).

verses.note: Named in Nehemiah's prayer among those, along with 'the rest of the prophets,' who tried to put him in fear.

characters.name: Eliashib the High Priest
characters.perkNote: Bonus themed around consecration and temple oversight — reflects his role sanctifying the Sheep Gate and later overseeing temple chambers.

children: Joiada (12:10; one of Joiada's own sons is the grandson identified in 13:28 as Sanballat's son-in-law)
genealogy.note: High priest; grandson of Jeshua, the high priest who returned earlier with Zerubbabel (12:10) — this Jeshua is a distinct person from the Levite named Jeshua active later in Nehemiah 8-9 (8:7; 9:4-5), a NAMING COLLISION worth flagging. Eliashib 'was allied unto Tobiah' by an unspecified relational tie (13:4) before giving him a temple chamber.

funFacts: As high priest he personally helped rebuild and sanctify the Sheep Gate (3:1) — and decades later personally furnished a temple chamber for one of the wall project's fiercest opponents (13:4-9).

verses.note: Rises up with his fellow priests and builds/sanctifies the Sheep Gate, setting up its doors.
Named in the high-priestly succession line: son of Joiakim, father of Joiada.
Having oversight of the temple chamber and being allied unto Tobiah, prepares him a great chamber there; Nehemiah later casts out all Tobiah's household stuff from it.
One of his grandsons (a son of Joiada) is found to have married Sanballat's daughter and is driven away by Nehemiah.

characters.name: Ezra the Scribe
characters.perkNote: Bonus themed around teaching and public reading of scripture — reflects his role reading and explaining the Law.

genealogy.note: Full genealogy is already established in the book of Ezra (7:1-5, tracing him to Aaron); not re-derived here since Nehemiah's own text does not restate it — he simply reappears as 'Ezra the scribe' / 'Ezra the priest.'

funFacts: Reads the Law aloud from morning until midday to a mixed crowd of men, women, and 'all that could hear with understanding' (8:2-3), from a specially built wooden pulpit (8:4).

verses.note: Brings the book of the Law before the congregation at the Water Gate and reads it aloud from morning to midday, with Levites helping the people understand.
Together with Nehemiah the Tirshatha and the Levites, tells the weeping people to instead rejoice and share portions.
Heads of the fathers' houses gather to him the next day to study the words of the Law further, and discover the instruction for the Feast of Tabernacles.
Leads one of the two processional companies at the wall dedication: 'and Ezra the scribe before them.'

characters.name: The Covenant Renewed
characters.purpose: A corporate confession reciting Israel's history of God's faithfulness against the nation's repeated unfaithfulness, leading the restored community to bind itself in a written, sealed document to specific renewed Torah obligations — no intermarriage with surrounding peoples, Sabbath observance, sabbatical-year debt release, a temple tax, wood offerings, and firstfruits/tithes for the priests and Levites (10:28-39). It exists to turn the public reading of the Law in chapter 8 into a formal, communal, signed commitment.
characters.deliveredBy: Led corporately by named Levites standing on the stairs (9:4: Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, Chenani; an adjacent list in 9:5 names Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah leading the people in blessing God). The resulting covenant document was then formally sealed, headed first by Nehemiah as Tirshatha, followed by the priests, Levites, and lay chiefs (10:1-27).
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around corporate commitment and discipline.

verses.note: The people assemble with fasting, sackcloth, and earth on their heads, separate from foreigners, and confess their sins and their fathers' iniquities.
Named Levites stand on the stairs and cry out, then call the people to stand and bless the LORD.

A long recital of Israel's history — creation, the patriarchs, the exodus, the wilderness, the conquest, the judges and kings, and the exile — as the basis for the nation's present distress and confession.
Because of all this, the people make a sure covenant in writing.
The sealed covenant document's signatories, headed by Nehemiah the Tirshatha, then priests, Levites, and chiefs of the people.
The specific terms sworn to: separation from foreign peoples, Sabbath and sabbatical-year observance, the temple tax, wood offering, firstfruits, and tithes for the Levites and priests.

characters.name: The Wall Dedication
characters.purpose: A public, citywide thanksgiving and purification ceremony marking the wall's completion, reuniting priests, Levites, singers, and musicians gathered from throughout the region into two processional companies that walk the wall in opposite directions before meeting at the temple — reaffirming the restored city's identity as a worship community, with the resulting joy 'heard even afar off' (12:43), not merely a fortified perimeter.
characters.deliveredBy: Organized personally by Nehemiah, who brought the princes of Judah onto the wall and appointed the two processional companies (12:31); one company was led by Ezra the scribe (12:36); the singers were overseen by Jezrahiah (12:42, indexed separately below); a group of priests played trumpets in the second company (12:41, undifferentiated list).
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around celebration and completion rewards.

verses.note: The Levites are sought out from their various towns to come celebrate the dedication with gladness, thanksgivings, singing, cymbals, psalteries, and harps.
Priests and Levites purify themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall.
The first thanksgiving company processes along the wall toward the dung gate, including Ezra the scribe before them.
The company continues past the fountain gate, the city of David, and around to the water gate.
Priests with trumpets and Levite singers, overseen by Jezrahiah, take part in the second company.
Great sacrifices are offered and the people rejoice, 'for God had made them rejoice with great joy... so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off.'

characters.name: Jezrahiah
characters.perkNote: Directly executes and supports the dedication ceremony Nehemiah organized.

genealogy.note: Named only once, as overseer of the singers at the wall dedication (12:42); no further identifying or family detail is given in the text.

verses.note: Oversees the singers, who 'sang loud' at the dedication.

characters.name: Artaxerxes
characters.perkNote: No mechanical perk assigned — an offstage enabling authority rather than an active participant in Jerusalem's own events.

genealogy.note: Persian king; his own dynastic genealogy is outside the scope of this book, which only records his direct exchanges with Nehemiah.

verses.note: Grants Nehemiah's request for leave, letters of safe passage, and timber for the building project, after noticing Nehemiah's sad countenance.
Referenced as the king in whose twentieth (through thirty-second) year Nehemiah served as governor of Judah without taking the governor's food allowance.
In his thirty-second year, Nehemiah requests and receives leave to return to Jerusalem a second time.

characters.name: Zerubbabel
characters.perkNote: No mechanical perk assigned in this book — referenced only as a chronology marker, not an active participant in Nehemiah's own narrative.

genealogy.note: Full genealogy is already established in the book of Ezra; referenced in Nehemiah only twice, both as an era/chronology marker ('in the days of Zerubbabel') rather than as an active participant in this book's events.

verses.note: Used to date the list of priests and Levites who came up with him and Jeshua at the earlier return.
Used again to date when the people gave the daily portions for singers and gatekeepers, 'in the days of Zerubbabel, and in the days of Nehemiah.'

genealogyLists.wall_builders_ch3: A roster of roughly 40+ named individuals and families who each repaired a specific section of the wall (Nehemiah 3), most with no further individual action beyond their assigned portion. Standouts already promoted to full entries: Eliashib the high priest (3:1). Notable but not promoted to full entries: Shallum the son of Halohesh repaired his section 'he, and his daughters' (3:12, unusual for naming daughters as builders); Baruch the son of Zabbai 'earnestly repaired' his section (3:20); the nobles of Tekoa 'put not their necks to the work of their Lord' — a pointed negative exception among otherwise willing builders (3:5). NAMING COLLISIONS within this chapter alone: at least two distinct men named Zadok (Zadok son of Baana, 3:4; Zadok son of Immer, 3:29) and at least two distinct men named Hananiah (3:8, 'son of one of the apothecaries'; 3:30, 'son of Shelemiah') — neither should be conflated with the separately-indexed Hananiah, ruler of the palace (7:2), or with the Hananiah among the priestly trumpeters at the wall dedication (12:41).
genealogyLists.law_teaching_levites_ch8_7: Thirteen Levites named as helping the people understand the Law as Ezra read it: Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodijah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, and Pelaiah (8:7). The text does not differentiate any individual's specific role within this group, so none is promoted to a full character entry per methodology's rule against inventing differentiation the text doesn't support.
genealogyLists.confession_prayer_levites_ch9: The Levites named leading the corporate confession from the stairs: Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani (9:4), with an adjacent, partly overlapping list in 9:5 — Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah. Attributed collectively as 'deliveredBy' on the Covenant Renewed law tier rather than individually indexed.
genealogyLists.covenant_sealers_ch10: Approximately 84 names sealing the covenant document (10:1-27), beginning with Nehemiah himself, then priests, Levites, and lay chiefs of the people. Bulk list, not individually indexed beyond Nehemiah, whose heading role is captured on his own character entry.
genealogyLists.returnees_census_ch7: Nehemiah 7:6-73 repeats the census of the first return under Zerubbabel with some numeric variation from the parallel list in Ezra 2 for a few individual clans — a recognized textual crux not resolved here. Not re-indexed individually in this book's roster.
genealogyLists.jerusalem_residents_ch11: Lists of families who settled in Jerusalem by a one-in-ten lot, plus the towns of Judah and Benjamin resettled by the rest (Nehemiah 11). Heads of families are named but without individual narrative action beyond the settlement list itself.
genealogyLists.priestly_trumpeters_dedication_12_41: Seven priests with trumpets at the wall dedication: Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah (12:41) — an undifferentiated group, attributed collectively under the Wall Dedication law tier. This Hananiah is distinct from the other Hananiahs flagged elsewhere in this book.
genealogyLists.priests_levites_lineage_12_1_26: A genealogical list of priests and Levites 'in the days of Zerubbabel,' including the high-priestly succession from Jeshua through Joiakim, Eliashib, Joiada, Jonathan/Johanan, to Jaddua (12:1-26). Establishes the high-priestly lineage Eliashib belongs to but is not individually indexed here beyond Eliashib himself.

notes:
Second-pass corrected redraft of Nehemiah. FIXED FIRST-DRAFT ISSUE: Nehemiah's own first-person action organizing and leading the wall dedication (12:31, plus 12:38 and 12:40) is now captured directly on Nehemiah's own character verse list, not only attributed to the Wall Dedication law tier (which still separately covers the ceremony's ritual details and credits Ezra's/Jezrahiah's roles).

Naming collisions flagged throughout (per methodology's explicit re-scan requirement): 'Nehemiah' itself is not unique in this book (distinct from Nehemiah son of Azbuk, 3:16, and a different, earlier Nehemiah among the first-return leaders, 7:7); at least two distinct men named Zadok (3:4, 3:29) besides Zadok the scribe/treasurer (13:13); at least four distinct men named Hananiah across the book (3:8; 3:30; 7:2, indexed as Nehemiah's submanager; 12:41); 'Shemaiah' is reused for several different men in this book alone (6:10, the hired false prophet, indexed here, vs. others in the wall-builder and priestly lists) — only the 6:10 false prophet is indexed as a character; Noadiah the prophetess (6:14) shares her name with an unrelated male Levite, Noadiah son of Binnui, in Ezra 8:33; Jeshua the high priest ancestor (12:10) is distinct from the Levite Jeshua active in chapters 8-9.

Hedged rather than resolved: the antecedent of 'he was a faithful man...feared God above many' in 7:2 is grammatically ambiguous between Hanani and Hananiah; Nehemiah 7's return-census totals are well known to diverge slightly from Ezra 2's parallel list for a few clans, a recognized textual crux not resolved here; Shemaiah's hiring by 'Tobiah and Sanballat' (6:12-13) is explicitly joint, and he is attached to Tobiah only because Tobiah is named first in that verse, not because the text assigns him more specifically to one over the other.

Not asserted: no age-at-event data is given for anyone in this book, so all ageEvents arrays are empty. Ezra's and Zerubbabel's fuller genealogies are treated as already established in the book of Ezra and are not re-derived here, consistent with the rule against resolving facts that depend on a different, unstated source when the present book itself doesn't restate them.
